title: Topic Modelling for Biomedical Literature Retrieval via a Dual-Stream Embedding Framework
abstract: The rapid expansion of biomedical literature has created substantial challenges in retrieving and synthesizing relevant knowledge, particularly for novice and interdisciplinary users. Conventional keyword-based methods often lack semantic depth, whereas traditional topic modelling techniques struggle to capture domain-specific contexts and rarely integrate structured metadata, such as medical subject headings (MeSH). To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.

title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.

title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

title: How Does SAM-3 Adapt? Capacity, Update Geometry, and Domain Transfer
abstract: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. Across these datasets, compact parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods often match or approach Full Fine-Tuning in DSC and IoU, suggesting that strong in-domain adaptation does not always require updating the full model. However, this performance cannot be explained by nominal adapter rank or trainable parameter count alone. To investigate why different methods perform similarly, we analyze their update spectra and their behavior under LoveDA Urban/Rural transfer. Our SVD analysis shows that Full Fine-Tuning updates are spectrally compressible. However, successful PEFT methods do not simply recover the same update directions; instead, they often concentrate changes in different components and subspaces. The domain-transfer study further shows that methods with similar in-domain performance can respond differently under distribution shift. Together, these results suggest that SAM-3 adaptation is often capacity-saturated in practice, while competitive fine-tuning arises through method-specific update paths rather than a single low-rank approximation to Full Fine-Tuning.

title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

title: Iterative optimization with partial convergence guarantees on neutral atom quantum computers
abstract: Neutral atom quantum computers (NAQCs) have emerged as a promising platform for solving the maximum weighted independent set (MWIS) problem. However, analog quantum approaches face two key limitations: constraints of the atomic layout on realizable graph geometries and the absence of performance guarantees. We introduce Lp-Quts, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that integrates an NAQC sampler into a classical cutting-plane algorithm. At each iteration, a relaxed linear program (RLP) bounds the MWIS and induces a reduced graph from which independent sets are sampled using an analog quantum sampler. A novel sample-informed separation problem guides odd-cycle cut selection and accelerates convergence. For t-perfect graphs, Lp-Quts inherits polynomial-time convergence guarantees from the classical theory of cutting planes. We evaluate our approach on instances with up to 300 vertices -- a scale that exceeds the capabilities of current NAQC hardware. In this regime, Lp-Quts reaches solutions within 5--10\% of optimality, outperforming direct analog quantum protocols and greedy baselines under equal sampling budgets. As expected, simulated annealing remains the strongest sample-based solver at this scale. These results demonstrate how quantum samplers can be effectively embedded within classical optimization frameworks to deliver near-optimal solutions with reduced quantum resources while preserving formal guarantees.

title: Word embeddings from text corpora: A simulation study on the representation of underlying structures
abstract: The grounding problem concerns how symbolic representations acquire meaning through connections to what they refer to. For word embeddings learned from text, a related empirical question is how much of the structure that generated the text they retain. This is difficult to test in natural corpora because that structure is generally unknown. We employed a microsimulation methodology to generate a controlled text corpus from a known spatial structure. A virtual language supermarket with 40 shelves organised into four departments (fruit, vegetables, beverages, extras) served as the generative environment. Product sequences from 80,000 simulated shoppers formed a corpus of 804,422 product selections, with each sequence unique. The GloVe algorithm was applied to this corpus to learn 50-dimensional word embeddings, which we compared with the network of shelves. Cosine distance between products correlated with their shortest-path distance in the network (Spearman ρ = 0.79 over all 7,140 product pairs, Mantel p = 0.001), and on average 61% of a product’s network neighbours were among its nearest neighbours in the embedding, against 7% expected by chance. Over ten independent simulations these values were 0.80 ± 0.01 and 0.62 ± 0.02, and shuffling words across the corpus removed the association. Raw co-occurrence counts, PPMI, SVD and word2vec also captured global distance structure but retrieved fewer neighbours (29–50%). Recovery was best with a context window of one word (ρ = 0.93) and was weaker for rare products. K-medoid clustering of all 120 products separated the fruit and extras departments completely, while vegetables and beverages, which are interleaved in the network, were mixed (adjusted Rand index 0.82). UMAP projections followed the network closely (ρ = 0.92) but distorted some parts of it. These findings show that distributional word embeddings can recover much of the structure that a generating process puts into co-occurrence statistics. They do not show that the embeddings are grounded in, or understand, what the words refer to. This controlled simulation provides a reproducible way to measure structural recovery by word embeddings.

title: BReD: BEV Residual Diffusion for Feed-Forward Road Gaussian Reconstruction
abstract: Accurate road surface reconstruction is essential for autonomous-driving mapping and simulation, but existing methods trade reconstruction quality for cross-scene inference. Optimization-based methods recover detailed surfaces through costly per-scene optimization, while feed-forward methods lack road-specific constraints and often produce large elevation errors. We propose \textbf{BReD}, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing road elevation, appearance, and semantics from calibrated six-camera sequences. BReD first estimates coarse elevation through LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only cameras at inference. A lightweight BEV residual diffusion model then conditions elevation refinement on a camera-derived depth--elevation discrepancy and elevation-aware image features. Diffusion-indexed perturbations expose the model to different discrepancy corruption levels during training, while inference performs one deterministic refinement from the clean discrepancy. The refined elevations are temporally aggregated to anchor road-aligned Gaussians, whose attributes are predicted by a geometry-prior-guided decoder without test-time optimization. On four held-out nuScenes scenes, BReD achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92\% semantic mIoU, compared with 14.43 cm for RoGS without test-time LiDAR and 8.88 cm for its test-time-LiDAR-assisted variant; both RoGS variants require per-scene optimization.

title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
abstract: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.

title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
abstract: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.

title: Quantum machine learning for the quantum lattice Boltzmann method: Trainability of variational quantum circuits for the nonlinear collision operator across multiple time steps
abstract: This study investigates the application of quantum machine learning (QML) to approximate the nonlinear component of the collision operator within the quantum lattice Boltzmann method (QLBM). To achieve this, we train a variational quantum circuit (VQC) to construct an operator $U$. When applied to the post-linear-collision quantum state $\ket{Ψ_i}$, this operator yields a final state $\ket{Ψ_f} = U\ket{Ψ_i}$ that successfully replicates the nonlinear collision dynamics derived from the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) approximation. Within this framework, we present two distinct architectures: the R1 model and the R2 model. The R1 model is designed for quantum simulations that involve multiple time steps without intermediate measurements, focusing on accurately capturing nonlinear dynamics in continuous evolution. In contrast, the R2 model is tailored to achieve the high-precision reconstruction of the nonlinear operator for a single time step with an unitary operator.

evidence.title: Quantum machine learning for the quantum lattice Boltzmann method: Trainability of variational quantum circuits for the nonlinear collision operator across multiple time steps
evidence.abstract: This study investigates the application of quantum machine learning (QML) to approximate the nonlinear component of the collision operator within the quantum lattice Boltzmann method (QLBM). To achieve this, we train a variational quantum circuit (VQC) to construct an operator $U$. When applied to the post-linear-collision quantum state $\ket{Ψ_i}$, this operator yields a final state $\ket{Ψ_f} = U\ket{Ψ_i}$ that successfully replicates the nonlinear collision dynamics derived from the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) approximation. Within this framework, we present two distinct architectures: the R1 model and the R2 model. The R1 model is designed for quantum simulations that involve multiple time steps without intermediate measurements, focusing on accurately capturing nonlinear dynamics in continuous evolution. In contrast, the R2 model is tailored to achieve the high-precision reconstruction of the nonlinear operator for a single time step with an unitary operator.

title: MoHA: Model-Conditioned Harness Adaptation for Long-Video Agents
abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.

title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.

title: Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsibilities, we define role integrity as the preservation of an agent's functional responsibilities when it acts on its subordinates' material. To measure it, we introduce RI-Bench, a behavioral benchmark grounded in the structures and public records of three institutional hierarchies: peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry. We choose these hierarchies because their rules explicitly assign the senior role a duty toward subordinate material, and together they cover three basic duties: to weigh, to verify, and to relay. Rather than scoring output correctness, we measure how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material, using rule-based checks and a rubric-guided LLM judge calibrated against human annotation. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 agentic episodes, senior agents rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but often follow a majority of generic reviews (up to 71% of decisions) or drop witnesses' stated limitations (up to 65% of cited claims). Obligation prompts reduce these failures without removing them, and they also shift behavior in the control conditions. These findings motivate direct, obligation-specific evaluation of role integrity rather than inferring it from general capability or explicit role instructions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jxtse/ri-bench.

title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

title: Quantum-enhanced Markov Chain Monte Carlo for Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Quantum computing offers an alternative paradigm for addressing combinatorial optimization problems compared to classical methods. However, despite recent hardware improvements, the execution of empirical quantum optimization experiments at scales known to be hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers is not yet in reach. In this work, we offer a different way to approach combinatorial optimization with near-term quantum computing. Motivated by the promising results observed in using quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) for approximating complicated probability distributions, we combine ideas of sampling from the device with QeMCMC together with warm-starting and parallel tempering, in the context of combinatorial optimization. We demonstrate empirically that our algorithm recovers the global optima for instances of the Maximum Independent Set problem (MIS) up to 117 decision variables using 117 qubits on IBM quantum hardware. We observe an indication of more favorable scaling relative to the tested classical MCMC methods on the chosen MIS instances. MIS is practically relevant across domains such as financial services and molecular biology. Although some MIS instances with a few hundred variables can be difficult for classical solvers, the instances studied here are solved efficiently by CPLEX.

title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
abstract: One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

title: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Subchunk Rollouts in Latent World Models
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.

title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $δ$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($δ$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($δ$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $δ$ = 1 minus $δ$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.

title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

title: Borrow the Style, Follow the Prompt: Progressive Reference-Guided Stylization
abstract: Reference-guided text-to-image stylization transfers visual appearance to content specified by text, but the reference subjects and backgrounds can interfere with what the generated image depicts. Suppressing this unwanted information can also discard transferable texture and material cues, creating a tension between content control and faithful preservation of the reference style. Accordingly, we propose ProStyle, which learns a content-suppressed style prior through cross-content supervision on same-style pairs with different subjects and backgrounds and injects it with weak conditioning at auxiliary layers to strengthen style expression. Building on this prior, a complementary pathway learns residual corrections from full reference patch features with the content-suppressed style pathway frozen, before both pathways undergo joint refinement under the same objective. For cross-content learning and evaluation, we introduce ReConStyle, which provides 134K training pairs, two test settings, and object-level measures of target-content fidelity and reference-object overlap alongside style similarity and text alignment. ProStyle outperforms all compared SD1.5-based baselines and achieves the best average rank of 1.86 across four automatic and three human-evaluation criteria on ReConStyle-Full. In the user study, it substantially outperforms the baselines in text alignment and combined suitability, with selection rates of 84.36% and 50.90%, respectively. On the external Style-Rank benchmark, it also achieves the highest CLIP-Text and ImageReward scores.

title: Cross-Platform Production Signatures of State-Linked Information Operations
abstract: An information operation active on several platforms presents different names, personas, and topics on each. Its working routine is harder to change. We call this routine the operation's production signature: the regularities in when and how its accounts post, reply, and repost. We measure it from timestamps and coarse action types only, using no content, profile metadata, or network ties, as timing and action profiles for accounts and learned action-gap policies for populations. We then ask which parts of a signature carry over to another platform and which belong to a single operation. We train models on Twitter archives of four state-linked operations and apply them to Internet Research Agency (IRA) accounts on Reddit, with no Reddit training labels. They rank the IRA accounts at AUC 0.90-0.94. Content detectors on the same route fall from 0.98 within a platform to 0.81. Daily phase accounts for most of the transfer. Posting volume reverses direction between platforms, and action mix follows the role accounts hold on each platform. What transfers is not unique to the IRA: a second operation shares the same working-hours window, and action-gap policies separate every operation from organic accounts (AUC 0.96-1.0) without consistently ranking their own operation first. On 938 Telegram channels, groups that forward the same sources keep ordinary hours and pace but publish original posts in the same ten-minute windows more often than chance. This pattern is invisible when accounts are examined one at a time. Our results suggest that timing and action traces learned on one platform can help flag likely operations on another.

title: SN-EDA: Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms (EDAs) converge prematurely on slopes, because truncation selection removes most of the variance along the gradient. The usual remedies enlarge the variance or shift the mean. We propose the skew-normal EDA (SN-EDA), which corrects the third moment instead. It samples from a skew-normal distribution whose skewness points along the cumulative path of the mean shifts, while the mean and covariance remain exactly the maximum-likelihood estimates. The estimation step is unchanged, and the skewness needs no control. On a linear function it raises the fraction of the variance that survives selection from 0.29 to 0.53. In a pre-registered test on 24 benchmark functions in 10, 20 and 40 dimensions the skewness, applied through a gate that the test finds dispensable, improves the Gaussian EDA significantly in five of six settings. When the population starts far from the optimum, the error, averaged logarithmically over a run, falls by one to three orders of magnitude, and the gain grows with the magnitude of the skewness as predicted. The skewness adds nothing to the anticipated mean shift, whose offspring distribution we show to be skewed already, and SN-EDA remains behind algorithms that also correct the second moment.

title: Reducibility of native weighted graphs on Rydberg arrays
abstract: We investigate the classical reducibility of random unit-disk graph (UDG) instances of the maximum independent set and maximum weighted independent set problems, which can be natively realized in Rydberg atom quantum processors. Using state-of-the-art kernelization techniques, we systematically probe how far classical preprocessing can simplify such native optimization problems of varying size and connectivity. While many small or sparse instances can be fully reduced, dense graphs often retain finite irreducible kernels even after extensive reductions. Introducing vertex weights tends to increase reducibility, whereas extending the interaction range in the underlying UDG connectivity suppresses the reduction efficiency. By exploring where classical reductions cease to be effective, we aim to delineate the regime of problem instances that remain computationally demanding—those most relevant for testing and benchmarking near-term quantum optimization hardware. We find that for the remaining finite kernels, quantum execution would require non-native embeddings with substantial resource overheads, suggesting that directly running native instances may be more practical than embedding a reduced kernel.

title: Recurrent neural networks implemented through spatiotemporal light propagation in optical fibers
abstract: Recurrent neural networks excel at temporal tasks and video processing but require energy-intensive sequential memory operations and algorithmic backpropagation through time. We demonstrate that multimode optical fibers naturally implement native spatiotemporal recurrent computation through passive light propagation. Spatially multiplexed video frames are encoded onto distinct optical channels with controlled time delays; these beams combine and recirculate through a fiber loop where Kerr nonlinearity-based couplings generate high-dimensional states encoding both current inputs and a fading memory. Remarkably, the entire optical system remains fixed with no trainable parameters or electronic feedback, yet this single physical configuration achieves competitive performance across diverse temporal and video-based machine learning tasks: chaotic time-series forecasting, human action recognition, steering angle prediction, and surgical skill assessment. Our results show that recurrent temporal processing can emerge directly from spatiotemporal wave dynamics. This paradigm shift from algorithmic to physical recurrence, enabled by intrinsic spatiotemporal nonlinearities of multimode fibers, offers a scalable, energy-efficient architecture for photonic machine learning.

title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.

title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a student model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B student models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning to Refine Actions with Visual Reliability and Tactile Feedback for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
abstract: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
abstract: Decision models score candidate answers in a single forward pass, but the intermediate reasoning that improves decision quality adds latency. title: Tracking Objects Through Assembly and Decomposition
abstract: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.

title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).

title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design
abstract: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs $1.7\times$ faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

title: Asuka-FM: A System-Architectural Co-Design Framework for Efficient Text-to-Image Pretraining on Consumer Hardware
abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.

title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

title: HumanCOIN: A 12,500-Hour Dataset for Human Intent in Egocentric Manipulation
abstract: First-person manipulation datasets treat the observation-action pair as the atomic unit and compress the generation and execution of an action into a policy network's weights, rendering the intent state behind the action unobservable. Human motor control research shows that intent mediates between observation and action and leaves observable traces along the intent pathway from decision to effect: gaze reaches the target before the hand, muscle load builds before contact, and cortical activity precedes the motor command. To record this pathway at scale, we present HumanCOIN, a first-person manipulation dataset built around human intent: 12,500 hours across 38 scene classes with three tiers of proxies. At the output end, the L1 attention tier (10,000 h) infers gaze from headband camera video, exposing the operator's next object of attention and reach before the hand moves. Midway, the L2 exertion tier (2,000 h) records surface EMG from armbands, making load expectations readable before execution is complete. At the origin, the L3 cognition tier (500 h) records scalp EEG, giving early readouts of task decisions and monitoring. Each tier inherits all proxies from the tiers below. The dataset further provides multi-view RGB images, depth maps and point clouds, 6-DoF head and wrist pose, and step-level action and object annotations. The controlled L3 setting additionally measures gaze, hand pose and finger kinematics directly. Clock and calibration data are released with the dataset so that any read rate can be re-aligned. The three tiers cover three stations, from visual orienting to cortical preparation, making the process behind visual-action pairs available for modeling at dataset scale. Project page: https://flagopen.github.io/HumanCOIN.

title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
abstract: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
abstract: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill$.$png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill$.$png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill$.$png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

title: DRVEXO-4B-Unified: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Speech-Vision System
abstract: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
